title: Modern Periodic Law and Modern Periodic Table
topicTitle: Modern periodic law, Moseley's experiment, and structure of modern periodic table
notes:
## 1. Introduction: why a table was needed at all
By 1860 chemists knew about sixty elements and had no reliable way to remember what any of them did. The situation was like a library where every book has a different spine and no catalogue: you can read a book you already hold, but you cannot find one you have not seen. The periodic table is that catalogue, and everything in this unit — blocks, groups, trends, even the shapes of the modern syllabus — is a consequence of the single idea that won: *arrange the elements by a number that governs their chemistry, and the chemistry repeats at regular intervals.*

**Everyday hook.** Nepal's cement plants, steel re-rolling mills and fertiliser blenders all live or die by a handful of elements — calcium in limestone, iron in ore, nitrogen fixed from air, potassium in potash. Choosing the right one from 118 is not memorisation; it is reading position on a grid: "group 2 carbonate decomposes on heating", "group 17 element is a strong oxidiser". The table converts 118 separate facts into about eighteen families.
## 2. Early attempts at classification: triads, octaves, curves and gaps

• **Dobereiner's Law of Triads (1829):** Grouped elements into triads where atomic mass of middle element was roughly arithmetic mean of first and third (e.g., Li 7, Na 23, K 39; Ca 40, Sr 88, Ba 137; Cl 35.5, Br 80, I 127). Failed because only a few triads could be identified.

• **Newlands' Law of Octaves (1865):** When elements are arranged in order of increasing atomic mass, every eighth element shows similar physical and chemical properties like musical notes (Sa, Re, Ga, Ma...). Failed after Calcium (valid only up to Ca, Z=20) and could not accommodate noble gases discovered later.

• **Lothar Meyer's Curve (1869):** Plotted atomic volume against atomic weight. Alkali metals occupied sharp peaks; alkaline earth metals occupied descending curves; halogens occupied ascending slopes; transition metals occupied valleys.

• **Mendeleev's Periodic Law (1869):** 'The physical and chemical properties of elements are periodic functions of their atomic masses.' Mendeleev left gaps for undiscovered elements (Eka-Boron = Scandium, Eka-Aluminium = Gallium, Eka-Silicon = Germanium). Anomalies: Inverted pairs (Ar 39.9 before K 39.1; Co 58.9 before Ni 58.7; Te 127.6 before I 126.9), no fixed position for Hydrogen, isotopes could not be accommodated.

![Mendeleev's 1871 periodic table, eight groups with gaps for undiscovered elements](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/a/aa/Periodic_table_by_Mendeleev%2C_1871.svg)

**Figure 3 — Mendeleev's table of 1871.** Eight vertical groups, elements ordered by atomic weight, and dashes where Mendeleev expected an undiscovered element (eka-boron, eka-aluminium, eka-silicon). *Source: Wikimedia Commons, [Periodic table by Mendeleev, 1871.svg](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Periodic_table_by_Mendeleev,_1871.svg), author NikNaks, public domain (PD-self).*

**What each early attempt got right and wrong.**

| Attempt | Basis | Worked for | Failed on | Lesson it taught |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Döbereiner triads (1829) | arithmetic mean of masses | Li/Na/K, Ca/Sr/Ba, Cl/Br/I | most elements form no triad | a *numerical* relation between members of a family exists |
| Newlands octaves (1865) | every eighth element repeats | light elements up to Ca | breaks down after Ca; forced into eight columns | periodicity is real but the *period length changes* |
| Lothar Meyer curve (1869) | atomic volume vs mass | alkali peaks, halogen troughs | gave no predictive scheme | the repetition is measurable, not imagined |
| Mendeleev (1869) | mass + chemical family, with gaps | predicted Ga, Ge, Sc | could not place H, isotopes, or the Ar/K pair | a table must be allowed to leave a hole |
## 3. Moseley and the modern periodic law
• English physicist Henry Moseley bombarded various metal anticathodes with high-speed cathode rays (electrons) and studied characteristic X-ray emission spectra.
• **Moseley's Law:** The square root of the frequency (√ν) of the characteristic X-ray spectral line is directly proportional to the atomic number (Z) of the target element:
$$\sqrt{\nu} = a(Z - b)$$
where ν = frequency of K_α X-ray line, Z = atomic number (nuclear charge), a and b are constants characteristic of the spectral line series (screening constant b ≈ 1 for K-series).

• **Fundamental Conclusion:** Plot of √ν vs Z yields a straight line, whereas plot of √ν vs atomic mass (A) does not. This conclusively proved that **atomic number (Z)**, representing the net positive nuclear charge (number of protons), is the fundamental property governing the chemical identity of elements, NOT atomic mass.
• **Statement of Modern Periodic Law:** 'The physical and chemical properties of elements are periodic functions of their atomic numbers.'

**Why the change of key mattered, in one sentence.** Mass is an average over isotopes, so it can be pulled in the wrong direction by abundance (Figure 2); nuclear charge is an exact integer that no isotope can alter. Replacing A by Z did not merely tidy the table — it made the ordering *physically meaningful*, because Z is the number of electrons in the neutral atom, and the electrons are what chemistry is made of.

**The modern periodic law, stated for the exam.** *The physical and chemical properties of the elements are periodic functions of their atomic numbers.* Every word matters: "periodic" (they repeat), "functions of Z" (not of mass), and "physical and chemical" (melting point and valency both obey it).
## 4. The anomalies Mendeleev could not solve, and how Z dissolves them

• **Anomalous Pairs Resolved:** Argon (Z=18) naturally precedes Potassium (Z=19); Cobalt (Z=27) naturally precedes Nickel (Z=28); Tellurium (Z=52) naturally precedes Iodine (Z=53) purely by increasing atomic numbers, regardless of atomic weights.
• **Position of Isotopes:** Since isotopes share identical atomic numbers (same Z, different mass number A), they occupy one single position in the periodic table without conflict.
• **Scientific Division into Blocks:** Reflects filling of electron shells according to quantum mechanics (Aufbau principle, Pauli exclusion, Hund's rule).

**Figure 2 — the three classic inversions.** Argon's average mass (39.95) exceeds potassium's (39.10) because argon is almost entirely ⁴⁰Ar, while potassium is 93 % ³⁹K. A mass-ordered table must therefore place K before Ar, contradicting the chemistry; a Z-ordered table places Ar (18) before K (19) and the chemistry is right. Cobalt/nickel and tellurium/iodine are the same story.

**The four anomalies in exam form.**

| Anomaly under mass ordering | Correct Z ordering | Physical reason |
| --- | --- | --- |
| K (39.10) should precede Ar (39.95) | Ar 18 before K 19 | argon is 99.6 % ⁴⁰Ar; potassium is 93 % ³⁹K |
| Co (58.93) should precede Ni (58.69) | Co 27 before Ni 28 | nickel's isotopes are lighter on average |
| Te (127.6) should precede I (126.9) | Te 52 before I 53 | tellurium's isotope mix is heavy |
| Isotopes have different masses | one box per element | same Z, same electron count, identical chemistry |
## 5. Structure of the long form: periods, groups and blocks
• **Periods (7 Horizontal Rows):** Corresponds to principal quantum number n of outermost valence shell.
- Period 1 (n=1): 2 elements (1s²)
- Period 2 (n=2): 8 elements (2s² 2p⁶)
- Period 3 (n=3): 8 elements (3s² 3p⁶)
- Period 4 (n=4): 18 elements (4s² 3d¹⁰ 4p⁶)
- Period 5 (n=5): 18 elements (5s² 4d¹⁰ 5p⁶)
- Period 6 (n=6): 32 elements (6s² 4f¹⁴ 5d¹⁰ 6p⁶, including Lanthanides ₅₈Ce–₇₁Lu)
- Period 7 (n=7): 32 elements (7s² 5f¹⁴ 6d¹⁰ 7p⁶, including Actinides ₉₀Th–₁₀₃Lr)

**Figure 1 — the four blocks of the long form.** The table is not an arbitrary grid: each block is the subshell being filled. Period 7 can hold 32 elements because the 5f, 6d, 7p and 7s subshells fill before 8s begins. Read the block from the configuration, and the group number follows arithmetically (§7–§8).

![Modern long-form periodic table colour-coded by s, p, d and f blocks](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/0/03/Simple_Periodic_Table_Chart-blocks.svg)

**Figure 4 — the modern 18-column table.** Compare this with Figure 3 to see what changed in 44 years: the groups doubled to 18, the f-block was pulled out below, and the ordering key became Z rather than mass. Read the colours as the four blocks of §5: s at the edges, d in the middle, p on the right, f detached. *Source: Wikimedia Commons, [Simple Periodic Table Chart-blocks.svg](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Simple_Periodic_Table_Chart-blocks.svg), author User:Double sharp (after Offnfopt), CC BY-SA 4.0 — attribution and share-alike required.*

**Reading the grid in one glance.** Rows are periods and equal *n*; columns are groups and equal *outer configuration*; colours are blocks and equal *subshell being filled*. A student who can say "period 4, group 16, p-block" for selenium has said, in one line, its shell number, its outer configuration (4s²4p⁴) and its family behaviour.

## 6. Why the periods have lengths 2, 8, 8, 18, 18, 32, 32
The length of a period is not a convention; it is the number of electrons the filling subshells can hold before the next period starts.

| Period | n | Subshells filled | Capacity sum | Length | First → last element |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 1 | 1s | 2 | 2 | H → He |
| 2 | 2 | 2s 2p | 2 + 6 | 8 | Li → Ne |
| 3 | 3 | 3s 3p | 2 + 6 | 8 | Na → Ar |
| 4 | 4 | 4s 3d 4p | 2 + 10 + 6 | 18 | K → Kr |
| 5 | 5 | 5s 4d 5p | 2 + 10 + 6 | 18 | Rb → Xe |
| 6 | 6 | 6s 4f 5d 6p | 2 + 14 + 10 + 6 | 32 | Cs → Rn |
| 7 | 7 | 7s 5f 6d 7p | 2 + 14 + 10 + 6 | 32 | Fr → Og |

**Formula.** A subshell of azimuthal quantum number *l* holds 2(2*l* + 1) electrons: s 2, p 6, d 10, f 14. Add the subshells that fill during a period and you get its length; summing the seven lengths gives **2 + 8 + 8 + 18 + 18 + 32 + 32 = 118**, the number of elements in the modern table.

**Why period 3 is only 8 while period 4 is 18.** After 3p comes 4s (lower in energy, because of penetration), so the 3d subshell waits until period 4. This single energy-ordering fact is why the table has a *gap* in the middle and why the transition series appears one period later than naive counting suggests.

## 7. Groups: eighteen columns and their IUPAC names
Since 1988 the columns are numbered 1–18, left to right, which replaces both the older European 0–VIII and the American IA–VIIIA conventions (the IUPAC naming rules themselves are in the next topic).

| Group | IUPAC collective name | Outer configuration | Family character | Example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | alkali metals | *n*s¹ | lose 1 e⁻, form M⁺, react with water | Na |
| 2 | alkaline earth metals | *n*s² | lose 2 e⁻, form M²⁺ | Ca |
| 3–12 | transition elements (d-block) | (*n*−1)d¹⁻¹⁰ *n*s¹⁻² | variable oxidation states, coloured ions, catalysts | Fe |
| 13 | boron family (icosagens) | *n*s²*n*p¹ | +3 state common | Al |
| 14 | carbon family (crystallogens) | *n*s²*n*p² | +4 / −4, covalent networks | Si |
| 15 | nitrogen family (pnictogens) | *n*s²*n*p³ | −3 to +5, lone pair available | N |
| 16 | oxygen family (chalcogens) | *n*s²*n*p⁴ | −2 typical, two lone pairs | O |
| 17 | halogens | *n*s²*n*p⁵ | gain 1 e⁻, form X⁻, strong oxidisers | Cl |
| 18 | noble gases | *n*s²*n*p⁶ (He 1s²) | closed shell, near-zero reactivity | Ar |

**The arithmetic that examiners love.** For an s-block element the group number *is* the number of outer s electrons; for a p-block element it is 10 + (s + p electrons); for a d-block element it is the sum of (*n*−1)d and *n*s electrons. Section 8 works this out for real elements.

## 8. Finding the period, block and group from a configuration
Three steps, always in this order:

1. **Period** = the highest principal quantum number present (the valence shell).
2. **Block** = the subshell receiving the last electron.
3. **Group** = arithmetic on the outer electrons, using the rule for that block.

| Element | Configuration | Period | Block | Group | Check |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Na (Z = 11) | [Ne]3s¹ | 3 | s | 1 | 1 s electron → group 1 |
| Mg (Z = 12) | [Ne]3s² | 3 | s | 2 | 2 s electrons → group 2 |
| Al (Z = 13) | [Ne]3s²3p¹ | 3 | p | 13 | 10 + (2 + 1) = 13 |
| S (Z = 16) | [Ne]3s²3p⁴ | 3 | p | 16 | 10 + (2 + 4) = 16 |
| Cr (Z = 24) | [Ar]3d⁵4s¹ | 4 | d | 6 | 5 + 1 = 6 |
| Cu (Z = 29) | [Ar]3d¹⁰4s¹ | 4 | d | 11 | 10 + 1 = 11 |
| Zn (Z = 30) | [Ar]3d¹⁰4s² | 4 | d | 12 | 10 + 2 = 12 |
| Br (Z = 35) | [Ar]3d¹⁰4s²4p⁵ | 4 | p | 17 | 10 + (2 + 5) = 17 |
| Ce (Z = 58) | [Xe]4f¹5d¹6s² | 6 | f | 3 (lanthanide) | f-block is placed in group 3 |

**Two traps.** (i) Chromium and copper are 3d⁵4s¹ and 3d¹⁰4s¹, not 3d⁴4s² and 3d⁹4s² — extra stability of half-filled and fully filled subshells; the *group* arithmetic still works because the 3d and 4s counts sum correctly. (ii) In the f-block the group number is not derived from electron count at all; lanthanides occupy period 6 group 3 by placement convention, and that convention is itself debated (§10).

## 9. Metals, non-metals and metalloids across the table
The metal/non-metal divide is not a group property but a *diagonal* one: it runs roughly from boron down to astatine.

| Class | Position | Count (of 118) | Typical properties | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Metals | left and centre; all of s, d, f blocks | about 91 (≈ 77 %) | malleable, conduct, form cations, basic oxides | Na, Fe, Cu, Pb |
| Non-metals | upper right, plus H | about 20 | brittle or gaseous, insulators, form anions, acidic oxides | O, S, Cl, C |
| Metalloids | the staircase: B, Si, Ge, As, Sb, Te | 6 (Po and At are debated) | semiconducting, amphoteric oxides | Si, Ge |

**The staircase, memorised as one line.** B–Si–Ge–As–Sb–Te, with the boundary running between Al/Si, between Ge/As diagonally, and between Po/At. Everything left of it is metal, everything right is non-metal, and silicon — the element the boundary runs through — is the reason semiconductors exist.

**Why the divide is diagonal.** Metallic character falls left → right across a period (Z rises, Zeff rises, electrons held more tightly) and rises down a group (shell number rises, Zeff nearly constant). Combining the two directions gives a diagonal boundary — the same diagonal that produces the diagonal relationships of Li/Mg and Be/Al in the periodic-trends topic.

## 10. Merits and limitations of the modern table
**Merits — say five.**
1. It is based on a measurable integer, Z, not on an average over isotopes, so no element can be misfiled.
2. It explains, rather than merely records, the Mendeleev anomalies (Ar/K, Co/Ni, Te/I) and gives isotopes a single position.
3. Block structure follows the Aufbau filling order, so the table encodes electron configuration.
4. The position of an element predicts its properties — group number gives valency, block gives ion type.
5. It accommodates all 118 known elements with no forced gaps, and predicted the properties of gaps before they were filled.

**Limitations — say four, and be precise.**
- **Hydrogen** is 1s¹ like an alkali metal but behaves as a non-metal (forms H⁻, H⁺ only as a bare proton in acid); it sits in group 1 by electron count, not by chemistry.
- **Helium** has the s² configuration of group 2 but the chemistry of group 18; it is placed in group 18 for behaviour, not configuration — the one place where the table's own rule is broken.
- **The f-block is detached.** Lanthanides and actinides are pulled out below the table, which hides the fact that they belong between groups 2 and 3 in periods 6 and 7.
- **Group 3 is unsettled.** Whether the third column contains La–Lu, Ac–Lr, or only Sc–Y–Lu/Lr is still argued; the IUPAC project on the question has not issued a binding ruling, so Nepali textbooks and Western ones can differ.
- The table does not explain *why* trends exist — that requires Zeff and shielding (next two topics). It records periodicity; it does not derive it.
## 11. IUPAC systematic names and symbols above Z = 100

• **IUPAC Nomenclature for Elements with Z > 100:** Uses numerical roots for digits: 0 = nil, 1 = un, 2 = bi, 3 = tri, 4 = quad, 5 = pent, 6 = hex, 7 = sept, 8 = oct, 9 = enn. Suffix '-ium'. Example: 104 = Unnilquadium (Unq), 118 = Ununoctium (Uuo / Oganesson).

**Worked, so the rule is usable.** Z = 118 → un + un + oct + ium → *ununoctium*, symbol Uuo; the element is now officially named **oganesson (Og)**. Z = 114 → ununquadium (Uuq) → now **flerovium (Fl)**. The systematic name is a placeholder that guarantees every new element has a usable name until IUPAC approves a permanent one.

| Digit | Root | Digit | Root |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | nil | 5 | pent |
| 1 | un | 6 | hex |
| 2 | bi | 7 | sept |
| 3 | tri | 8 | oct |
| 4 | quad | 9 | enn |

**Trap.** Before a root beginning with *i* (1, 8, 9), the connecting *i* of "-ium" is dropped: Z = 119 is *ununennium* (Uue), not "ununennnium". The symbol takes the first letter of each root, capitalised: Uue.

confusion: ❌ Modern Periodic Law is based on atomic mass like Mendeleev's law. ✅ Modern Periodic Law is strictly based on atomic number (Z), discovered by Moseley via X-ray spectroscopy.
❌ Isotopes need separate positions in the modern periodic table. ✅ Isotopes possess identical atomic numbers, so they naturally share the exact same slot in the modern table.

❌ Cobalt was placed before Nickel by Mendeleev as an error. ✅ Mendeleev placed Co before Ni based on chemical properties despite Co being heavier (58.93 vs 58.69); modern table confirms Co (Z=27) correctly precedes Ni (Z=28).
❌ Moseley's graph plotted frequency ν against atomic weight. ✅ Moseley plotted the square root of frequency (√ν) against atomic number (Z), obtaining a perfect straight line: √ν = a(Z - b).
❌ Period number corresponds to total number of electrons. ✅ Period number corresponds directly to the principal quantum number (n) of the outermost valence electron shell.
❌ The modern table still lists elements by atomic weight. ✅ It lists them by Z; the mass order breaks at Ar/K, Co/Ni and Te/I.
❌ Period length is a convention chosen by IUPAC. ✅ It follows from subshell capacity: 2(2l+1) summed over the subshells filled.
❌ Helium belongs to group 2 because it has two outer electrons. ✅ It is group 18 because its filled 1s shell gives noble-gas chemistry.

universalFacts: Henry Moseley established atomic number as the genuine identity of chemical elements in 1913, shortly before dying in World War I at age 27.
The 7 periods of the modern table correspond exactly to principal energy levels n = 1 to 7.
Periodicity in chemical properties arises from the periodic recurrence of similar valence shell electronic configurations.
numericals:
**N1 — Total number of elements in the long form.**
*Given.* Period lengths 2, 8, 8, 18, 18, 32, 32.
*Formula.* Total = Σ (period length).
*Substitution.* 2 + 8 + 8 + 18 + 18 + 32 + 32 = 118.
*Answer.* **118 elements** occupy the seven periods of the modern table.

**N2 — Why period 7 stops at 32.**
*Given.* The subshells filled during period 7 are 7s, 5f, 6d, 7p; capacities are 2(2*l* + 1) = 2, 14, 10, 6.
*Formula.* Length = 2 + 14 + 10 + 6.
*Substitution.* 2 + 14 + 10 + 6 = 32.
*Answer.* **32 elements** (Fr, Z = 87 → Og, Z = 118), which is exactly 118 − 86.

**N3 — Position of bromine from its configuration.**
*Given.* Z = 35; configuration [Ar]3d¹⁰4s²4p⁵.
*Formula.* Period = highest n; block = last subshell filled; group (p-block) = 10 + (s + p outer electrons).
*Substitution.* Highest n = 4 → period 4; last subshell 4p → p-block; group = 10 + (2 + 5) = 17.
*Answer.* **Period 4, group 17, p-block** — check: Br is the third halogen, two rows below F, as expected.

**N4 — Metals in the table, as a percentage.**
*Given.* Approximately 91 of the 118 elements are metals.
*Formula.* Percentage = (metals / total) × 100.
*Substitution.* (91 / 118) × 100 = 77.1 %.
*Answer.* **≈ 77 %** of the elements are metals — the reason "typical element" in a chemistry exam usually means a metal.

**N5 — Using Moseley's law to compare two Kα lines.**
*Given.* √ν = a(Z − b) with b = 1 for the K series; copper Z = 29, iron Z = 26.
*Formula.* ν ∝ (Z − 1)², so ν(Cu)/ν(Fe) = [(29 − 1)/(26 − 1)]².
*Substitution.* (28/25)² = 1.2544.
*Answer.* Copper's Kα frequency is **1.25 times** iron's, i.e. about 25 % higher; the wavelength ratio is the inverse, λ(Cu)/λ(Fe) = 0.797.

**N6 — Counting the f-block.**
*Given.* Lanthanides run from Ce (Z = 58) to Lu (Z = 71) inclusive; actinides from Th (Z = 90) to Lr (Z = 103).
*Formula.* Count = Z(last) − Z(first) + 1.
*Substitution.* 71 − 58 + 1 = 14; 103 − 90 + 1 = 14.
*Answer.* **14 lanthanides and 14 actinides**, matching the 4f and 5f capacities of 14 electrons each.

mcs.question: The modern periodic law arranges elements in order of:
mcs.explanation: Moseley's X-ray work (1913) showed √ν ∝ (Z − b), making Z the ordering key; mass ordering fails at Ar/K, Co/Ni and Te/I.

mcs.question: Moseley's law for characteristic X-rays is written as:
mcs.explanation: The square root of the frequency is linear in Z, which is why a plot of √ν against Z is a straight line but a plot against atomic mass is not.

mcs.question: The number of elements in the sixth period is:
An element with configuration [Ar]3d¹⁰4s²4p³ belongs to:
mcs.explanation: Highest n = 4; last subshell 4p; group = 10 + (2 + 3) = 15. The element is arsenic.

mcs.question: Which pair is correctly ordered only when Z, not mass, is used?
mcs.explanation: Te has the larger average mass (127.6) but the smaller atomic number; a mass-ordered table would invert the pair.

mcs.question: The number of columns in the long-form table, and the block of group 12, are respectively:
mcs.explanation: IUPAC numbers the columns 1–18; groups 3–12 are the d-block, group 12 (Zn, Cd, Hg) included.

mcs.question: Argon's average atomic mass (39.95) exceeds potassium's (39.10) mainly because:
options: argon is almost entirely ⁴⁰Ar while potassium is mostly ³⁹K
argon has a larger atomic radius
mcs.explanation: Average mass is an isotope-abundance average, so it is not a reliable ordering key; Z is exact.

mcs.question: Helium is placed in group 18 although its configuration is 1s². The reason is:
options: it has two valence electrons like group 2
its filled 1s shell gives noble-gas behaviour
mcs.explanation: This is the one place where the table's own configuration rule is overridden by chemical behaviour.

mcs.question: Which set contains only metalloids?
mcs.explanation: The staircase runs B–Si–Ge–As–Sb–Te; aluminium and gallium are metals, selenium and tellurium are borderline with Te usually counted.

mcs.question: For an element of the third period with configuration 3s²3p⁴, the group number is:
mcs.explanation: p-block rule: group = 10 + (s + p) = 10 + (2 + 4) = 16; the element is sulphur.

summary: The modern table orders elements by atomic number Z, the key Moseley established from characteristic X-ray frequencies (√ν = a(Z − b)). Ordering by Z resolves the three classic inversions (Ar/K, Co/Ni, Te/I) and gives isotopes a single box. The seven periods hold 2, 8, 8, 18, 18, 32, 32 = 118 elements, each length being the capacity of the subshells that fill during that period. Eighteen IUPAC columns group elements by outer configuration: 1–2 s-block, 3–12 d-block, 13–18 p-block, with the f-block detached below. Period, block and group can be read off a configuration in three steps. Metals occupy the left and centre (about 77 % of all elements), non-metals the upper right, and the metalloids form the B–Si–Ge–As–Sb–Te staircase. Hydrogen, helium, the detached f-block and the unsettled group-3 question are the table's standing limitations.
keyPoints: Modern periodic law: properties are periodic functions of atomic number, not atomic mass.
Moseley's law √ν = a(Z − b) fixed Z as the ordering key in 1913.
Period lengths: 2, 8, 8, 18, 18, 32, 32 — sum 118; each equals 2(2l+1) summed over the subshells that fill.
18 columns: groups 1–2 s-block, 3–12 d-block, 13–18 p-block, f-block detached below.
Group rules: s → count s electrons; p → 10 + (s + p); d → (n−1)d + ns.
Metals ≈ 77 % of the table; the non-metal boundary is the B–Si–Ge–As–Sb–Te staircase.
Limitations: hydrogen's position, helium in group 18, detached f-block, unsettled group 3.
